schema_ddl:
CREATE TABLE PAYROLL (SSNO INT, DEPTNO INT);
CREATE TABLE APPLICANT (SSNO INT, JOBTITILE INT, OFFICENO INT);
q1: SELECT Y.* FROM PAYROLL AS X, APPLICANT AS Y WHERE X.SSNO = Y.SSNO AND X.DEPTNO = 29
q2: SELECT C.* FROM PAYROLL AS A, (SELECT Y.SSNO, Y.DEPTNO FROM PAYROLL AS Y) AS B, APPLICANT AS C WHERE A.SSNO = B.SSNO AND C.SSNO = A.SSNO AND B.DEPTNO = 29
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT Y.* FROM PAYROLL AS X, APPLICANT AS Y WHERE X.SSNO = Y.SSNO AND X.DEPTNO = 29
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT C.* FROM PAYROLL AS A, (SELECT Y.SSNO, Y.DEPTNO FROM PAYROLL AS Y) AS B, APPLICANT AS C WHERE A.SSNO = B.SSNO AND C.SSNO = A.SSNO AND B.DEPTNO = 29
counterexample: INSERT INTO PAYROLL (SSNO, DEPTNO) VALUES (1001, 29); INSERT INTO PAYROLL (SSNO, DEPTNO) VALUES (1002, 30); INSERT INTO APPLICANT (SSNO, JOBTITILE, OFFICENO) VALUES (1001, 1, 101); INSERT INTO APPLICANT (SSNO, JOBTITILE, OFFICENO) VALUES (1002, 2, 102);
explanation: Q1 retrieves all columns from APPLICANT for rows where SSNO matches between PAYROLL and APPLICANT, and DEPTNO = 29. Q2 has an unnecessary subquery that selects from PAYROLL again but does not filter the subquery result with DEPTNO = 29. This means Q2 could return more rows than Q1 if DEPTNO = 29 is not enforced on the subquery.
counterexample_dsp: A test case with two rows in PAYROLL: one with DEPTNO = 29 and one with DEPTNO = 30, both matching SSNO values in APPLICANT. Q1 returns only the row with DEPTNO = 29, but Q2 may return both due to the subquery not filtering on DEPTNO = 29.
